lines.say: Forty-one projects.
Thirty judges.
One hundred and twenty-six reviews.
One winner.
But can you prove they deserved to win?
This is Dogfood Judge. Results you can defend.
Judge A loves everything. Nines and tens.
Judge B is tough. Fives and sixes.
Judge C gives almost everyone a seven.
The usual approach: average the scores, sort, declare a winner.
But judges don't use the scale the same way. Draw the harsh judge, and you lose on luck.
What if one review changed the winner? What if removing one judge flips it?
I built Dogfood Judge to answer those questions.
It's a complete, self-hosted hackathon platform: Go, SQLite, and Next.js.
Events, teams, submissions, assignments, scoring, analysis, publishing, and verification.
But the real work happens after scoring.
Assignments respect tracks, conflicts of interest, and load balance.
Now, what if one judge asks for another judge's scores?
The backend refuses. Four oh three.
Isolation is enforced by the server, not hidden by the UI. A forty-four case authorization matrix proves it.
lines.text: Isolation is enforced by the server, not hidden by the UI. A 44-case authorization matrix proves it.

lines.say: Now, the judging engine.
A raw score mixes two things: how good the project is, and how generous its judges were.
Dogfood models each judge's leniency and scale, using the overlap between judges.
Corrections are shrunk with empirical Bayes, so sparse judges aren't over-corrected.
And every rank comes with error bars: a rank interval, and the probability of a top three finish.
Which brings us to the question every losing team asks.
Is the winner defensible?
Dogfood removes each judge in turn and refits the whole model. Thirty refits.
lines.text: Dogfood removes each judge in turn and refits the whole model. 30 refits.

lines.say: On the sample event, first place survives twenty-four of thirty. Six specific judges can change the winner.
lines.text: On the sample event, first place survives 24 of 30. Six specific judges can change the winner.

lines.say: The lead over second place? Zero point zero five standard errors.
lines.text: The lead over second place? 0.05 standard errors.

lines.say: Other platforms print first place and move on. Dogfood says it's a coin flip, and how to settle it.
Next, reviews that disagree with everyone.
The model predicts every review. Reviews it can't explain get flagged.
In our test suite, one planted rogue review moved a project from nineteenth to twenty-ninth.
lines.text: In our test suite, one planted rogue review moved a project from #19 to #29.

lines.say: It doesn't just flag a review. It measures what that review cost.
When the podium is close, reviewing everything again is waste.
Most projects are already settled, near zero or near one hundred percent.
lines.text: Most projects are already settled, near 0% or near 100%.

lines.say: The tie-breaker round finds the coin flips at the prize line, and adds a judge to each.
Judge time goes where another review can actually change the outcome.
Sometimes a score isn't enough. So there's a pairwise mode.
A judge sees two projects. A, B, or tie.
The server picks the pairs adaptively, so no judge can steer them.
Verdicts are fitted with Bradley Terry, a regularizing prior, and real standard errors.
lines.text: Verdicts are fitted with Bradley–Terry, a regularizing prior, and real standard errors.

lines.say: Fairness is half the story. The other half is trust.
Publishing produces a signed bundle: pseudonymized inputs, a fingerprint, an audit anchor, and the ranking.
Anyone can run dogfood verify results. It re-runs the exact engine, offline.
lines.text: Anyone can run dogfood verify-results. It re-runs the exact engine, offline.

lines.say: Verified.
Now change a single score, and run it again.
Verification failed. The fingerprint no longer matches.
Judges can even verify their own reviews in the browser, with Merkle proofs.
And it's all tested end to end.
The Go suite boots the real portal. Real SQLite, real HTTP, not mocks.
The organizers' checker passes tiers one and two. Ours covers three and four.
lines.text: The organizers' checker passes T1 and T2. Ours covers T3 and T4.

lines.say: Authorization, deadlines, conflicts of interest, tamper detection, CSRF, CSV injection, rate limits, and signed webhooks.
And it all runs on your own machine.
One command. Docker compose up.
After the first build, pull the network. It keeps running, with zero outbound requests.
So let's go back to that leaderboard.
This time, the winner comes with evidence.
Picking a winner is easy.
Proving the result is fair is harder.
I'm Prince Panchani. This is Dogfood Judge. Results you can defend.
